items.title: What moves an option's price
items.core_explanation_md:
Five factors, and how a **rise** in each affects the price:

| Factor rises | Call price | Put price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strike price | Falls | Rises |
| Time to maturity | Rises | Rises |
| Stock (underlying) price | Rises | Falls |
| Risk-free interest rate | Rises | Falls |
| Volatility | Rises | Rises |

Why volatility helps both: the holder is protected against bad moves (can walk away) but gains from favourable ones, so more uncertainty adds value to either right. Why time helps both: more time means more chance of a favourable move.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Before maturity an option has **time value** on top of its intrinsic value (the difference between stock and strike, if favourable). Time value shrinks to zero at maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: A stock's volatility doubles. What happens to the call and put prices?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both rise, because greater uncertainty makes either right more valuable.

items.title: Option value bounds and the two pricing models
items.core_explanation_md:
An option never has negative value, and arbitrage fixes a floor:

- **Call**: worth at least the stock price minus the **present value** of the strike, and never less than zero: max[0, S - PV(K)].
- **Put**: worth at least PV(K) - S (or zero).

Two models give the exact price.

- **Binomial model**: price moves at discrete steps, up or down by set percentages with probabilities p and 1 - p; the number of up moves is binomial.
- **Black-Scholes model**: price moves continuously and returns are normal; the call value uses the standard normal cumulative N(d1) and N(d2) with d1 and d2 built from the stock price, strike, rate, volatility and time.

The put follows from put-call parity: P = K e to the minus r(T - t) minus S plus C.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A trader compares the market price with the model value: buy options priced below it, sell those priced above. The details of the formulas are beyond hand calculation; understand the inputs and the direction of each effect.

formula_spec.latex_expression: C \ge \max[0,\ S - PV(K)],\quad P \ge PV(K) - S,\quad C = N(d_1)S - N(d_2)Ke^{-r(T-t)},\quad P = Ke^{-r(T-t)} - S + C

variables.name: Present value of the strike, K discounted at the risk-free rate
Risk-free rate, volatility and time to expiry

assumptions: Black-Scholes: continuously moving prices and normally distributed returns.
The bounds hold for the stated option style and no arbitrage.
common_errors: Using the strike price instead of its present value in the bound.
Forgetting the floor at zero.
Using N(d2) in place of N(-d2) when writing the put directly (use put-call parity).

self_check.prompt_text: Stock Rs 120, strike Rs 100, discount factor 1/1.05. What is the lower bound for the call?

items.title: Estimating: point, interval, estimator and estimate
items.core_explanation_md:
We seldom know a population value (the average balance of **all** accounts, the share of **all** loans that will turn bad). We take a sample and **infer**.

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Estimator** | The sample statistic used (a formula or rule) | The sample mean |
| **Estimate** | The number that formula gives for one sample | Rs 18,400 |
| **Point estimate** | A single value | "The average balance is Rs 18,400" |
| **Interval estimate** | A range, with a probability attached | "Between Rs 17,900 and Rs 18,900, with 95 per cent confidence" |

A point estimate is either right or wrong, and it does not tell you how wrong. An interval estimate tells you both the likely **size of the error** (its width) and **how sure** you are (its probability).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Statistics has two main tools of inference: **estimation** (this unit) and **testing of hypotheses**. Estimation asks "what is the value?"; testing asks "is this claim about the value plausible?"

self_check.prompt_text: Is "the sample mean" an estimator or an estimate? And "Rs 18,400 from this sample"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The sample mean is an estimator (the rule); Rs 18,400 is an estimate (its value in one sample).

items.title: Four marks of a good estimator
items.core_explanation_md:
| Property | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Unbiased** | On average it hits the target: the mean of its sampling distribution equals the parameter, so it is not systematically too high or too low |
| **Efficient** | Among competing estimators it varies least from sample to sample, that is, it has the **smaller standard error** |
| **Consistent** | As the sample grows it gets almost certainly very close to the parameter |
| **Sufficient** | It uses all the information the sample holds about the parameter |

Example of efficiency: for samples of the same size the sample mean has a standard error of 1.05 and the sample median 1.6. The mean is the more efficient estimator of the population mean.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Consistency also tells you whether a bigger sample will help. If an estimator is not consistent, taking more observations wastes time and money.

self_check.prompt_text: Estimator A has a standard error of 2.0 and estimator B of 3.5, both unbiased. Which is more efficient, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A: with the same bias (none), the smaller standard error means less variation from sample to sample.

items.title: Point estimators of the mean, variance and proportion
items.core_explanation_md:
Three standard point estimators:

- **Mean**: the sample mean estimates the population mean.
- **Variance**: add the squared deviations from the sample mean and divide by **n - 1**, not n. Dividing by n gives an estimator that is biased (it tends to be too small), while dividing by n - 1 makes it **unbiased**.
- **Proportion**: the sample proportion p-bar = (number with the characteristic) / n estimates the population proportion.

The standard deviation estimate is the square root of the variance estimate.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Earlier, when describing a data set that was the whole population, the divisor was N. Here the data are a sample drawn to say something about a bigger population, so the divisor is n - 1.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \hat{\mu} = \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n},\quad s^2 = \frac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2}{n-1},\quad \bar{p} = \frac{x}{n}
assumptions: Simple random sample from the population.
n is at least 2 for a variance estimate.
common_errors: Dividing by n when estimating a population variance from a sample.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.
Counting the population size in place of n.

self_check.prompt_text: Five readings have squared deviations adding to 90. What is the estimate of the population variance?

items.title: Confidence levels and confidence intervals
items.core_explanation_md:
A **confidence interval** is a sample mean plus or minus a multiple of the standard error:

**x-bar plus or minus z x (standard error)**, where z is chosen by how confident you want to be.

| Confidence level | z (standard errors either side) |
| --- | --- |
| 68.3 per cent | 1 |
| 90 per cent | 1.64 |
| 95 per cent | 1.96 |
| 95.5 per cent | 2 |
| 99 per cent | 2.58 |
| 99.7 per cent | 3 |

The ends are the **lower** and **upper confidence limits**.

**Trade-off.** More confidence needs a wider interval, and a wide interval is less precise. A 99 per cent interval is surer but fuzzier than a 90 per cent one.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A bank manager who wants a very precise estimate must accept less confidence, or take a bigger sample (which shrinks the standard error).

self_check.prompt_text: Which is wider, a 90 per cent or a 99 per cent interval from the same sample, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The 99 per cent interval: it uses 2.58 standard errors each side instead of 1.64, to be more sure of containing the parameter.

items.title: Reading a confidence interval correctly
items.core_explanation_md:
The population mean is a **fixed number**. It does not move; your interval does, from sample to sample.

So it is wrong to say "there is a 95 per cent chance that the mean lies in this interval". Say instead: **if we drew many samples and built an interval from each in the same way, about 95 per cent of those intervals would contain the true mean.** This particular interval either contains it or it does not; the 95 per cent describes the method.

A picture to hold: five intervals drawn from five samples; four catch the true mean, one misses.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In practice we have one sample and one interval, and we say we are 95 per cent confident because the method works 95 times in 100.

self_check.prompt_text: What does "95 per cent confident" describe: this one interval, or the method of building intervals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The method: about 95 per cent of intervals built this way contain the population mean.

items.title: Interval estimate of a mean from a large sample (sigma known)
items.core_explanation_md:
With a large sample (n above 30) the sample mean is approximately normal even if the population is not. So:

1. Find the standard error: sigma divided by the square root of n.
2. Pick z for the confidence level.
3. Add and subtract z standard errors from the sample mean.

Example shape: n = 100, mean 21 months, sigma 6 months. Standard error 0.6. For 95 per cent confidence the margin is 1.96 x 0.6 = 1.18, so the interval is 19.82 to 22.18 months.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The margin (z times the standard error) is the same on both sides. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error and so halves the margin.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \bar{x} \pm z\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
assumptions: Simple random sample, n above 30.
Population standard deviation known.
Infinite population, or a sample under 5 per cent of a finite one.
common_errors: Using sigma instead of sigma over the square root of n as the margin.
Choosing the wrong z for the confidence level.
Applying the formula to a small sample from a non-normal population.

self_check.prompt_text: Sample mean 50, sigma 12, n = 36, 95 per cent confidence. What are the limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Standard error 2; margin 1.96 x 2 = 3.92; limits 46.08 and 53.92.

items.title: When sigma is unknown, or the population is small
items.core_explanation_md:
Two practical complications:

**sigma unknown.** Replace sigma by the sample standard deviation s, computed with divisor n - 1 (called sigma-hat).

**finite population.** If you sample more than 5 per cent of a finite population without replacement, shrink the standard error with the finite population multiplier:

estimated standard error = (sigma-hat over root n) x root of ((N - n) / (N - 1)).

Then build the interval as before.

Example: 700 families, sample 50, mean Rs 11,800, s = Rs 950. The sample is 7 per cent of the population, so the multiplier applies; the estimated standard error is Rs 129.57 and the 90 per cent limits are Rs 11,587.50 to Rs 12,012.50.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Skipping the multiplier when it is needed overstates the standard error and gives an interval that is wider than necessary.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \hat{\sigma}_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}},\qquad \bar{x} \pm z\,\hat{\sigma}_{\bar{x}}

variables.name: Sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1) used as the estimate of sigma

assumptions: Finite population, sampling without replacement, n/N above 0.05.
Large sample (n above 30).
common_errors: Using divisor n for the sample standard deviation.
Applying the multiplier when the sample is under 5 per cent of the population.
Using the multiplier's square root incorrectly (N - n over N - 1, not N - n over N).

self_check.prompt_text: N = 100 and n = 25. Does the finite population multiplier apply, and what is its value?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes: 25 per cent is above 5 per cent. sqrt(75/99) = 0.8704.

items.title: Interval estimate of a proportion from a large sample
items.core_explanation_md:
Counting successes follows the binomial distribution, but for a large enough sample the **normal** distribution approximates it. The rule of thumb: both n times p and n times q must be **at least 5**.

Steps:

1. Sample proportion p-bar; q-bar = 1 - p-bar.
2. Estimated standard error = square root of (p-bar x q-bar / n).
3. Limits: p-bar plus or minus z standard errors.

Example: 75 employees, 40 per cent prefer their own retirement plan. Estimated standard error = sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 75), about 0.0566. At 99 per cent confidence (z = 2.58) the limits are about 0.254 and 0.546.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware rounds the standard error to 0.057 first, which gives limits 0.253 and 0.547. Rounding at the end gives 0.254 and 0.546; either way the story is the same.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \hat{\sigma}_{\bar{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{\bar{p}\bar{q}}{n}},\qquad \bar{p} \pm z\,\hat{\sigma}_{\bar{p}}
assumptions: n p-bar and n q-bar both at least 5.
Simple random sample.
common_errors: Using the formula when n times p-bar or n times q-bar is below 5.
Forgetting to take the square root.
Expressing limits in per cent in one place and as a fraction in another.

self_check.prompt_text: n = 100 and p-bar = 0.4. What is the estimated standard error of the proportion?

items.title: What a linear programme is, and when it applies
items.core_explanation_md:
Linear programming decides **how much of each activity to do** when resources are limited, so as to get the best possible result.

| Part | Meaning | Banking example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Decision variables** | The quantities to be decided | Number of home loans and vehicle loans to process |
| **Objective function** | The measure to maximise or minimise | Total profit, or total cost |
| **Constraints** | Limits the plan must respect | Officer hours, documentation hours, funds available |
| **Non-negativity** | Variables cannot be below zero | You cannot process minus five loans |

For the method to apply, four conditions must hold: everything is **linear** (double the activity, double the use of resource and the profit), data are **known and certain**, variables are **non-negative**, and activity levels are **divisible**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If profit per unit falls as volume rises, or if a resource requirement is uncertain, a plain linear programme is not the right model. The divisibility condition is why you may get an answer like 2.67 loans: round it with care, or use a method for whole numbers.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank's profit per loan drops by half once more than 50 loans are processed. Which LP condition fails?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Linearity (proportionality): profit per unit is not constant, so the objective is not linear in the number of loans.

items.title: Formulating a problem: a four-step checklist
items.core_explanation_md:
Turn the words into mathematics in this order:

1. **Name the decision variables** (x = home loans per week, y = vehicle loans per week).
2. **Write the objective** as a linear function (profit 4x + 3y, in Rs thousand).
3. **Write one constraint per limited resource**: resource used by all activities is at most (or at least) what is available. Home loans need 3 officer-hours and vehicle loans 2: 3x + 2y is at most 120.
4. **Add non-negativity**: x and y are at least 0.

Each "at most" constraint is a ceiling, each "at least" constraint a floor. Units must match on both sides.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A common slip is a constraint that mixes units (hours on the left, rupees on the right) or a missing non-negativity condition, which lets the model choose a negative quantity.

self_check.prompt_text: Documentation takes 1 hour per home loan and 2 hours per vehicle loan, with 60 hours available. Write the constraint.
self_check.expected_takeaway: x + 2y is at most 60.

items.title: The graphical method: feasible region and corner points
items.core_explanation_md:
With two decision variables you can draw the problem.

1. Draw each constraint as a line. Shade the side that satisfies it.
2. The overlap of all shaded sides (in the first quadrant) is the **feasible region**: every point in it is a plan that obeys all the limits.
3. Draw an **iso-profit line**: all the combinations that earn the same profit. Slide it away from the origin, keeping its slope, until it is about to leave the region.
4. The last point touched is the **optimum**. It is a **corner (extreme point)** of the region.

Because an optimum is always at a corner (if it exists), you can skip the sliding and simply **evaluate the objective at each corner** and pick the best.

Exception: if the iso-profit line is parallel to a boundary, every point on that edge is optimal: many solutions with the same profit.
items.expanded_explanation_md: At the optimum corner, the constraints that meet there are fully used (binding). The others usually have spare room.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is it enough to check only the corner points?
self_check.expected_takeaway: If an optimum exists, at least one lies at a corner of the feasible region, and there are only a few corners.

items.title: Standard form for the simplex method: slack variables
items.core_explanation_md:
The simplex method works on equations, not inequalities. So turn every "at most" constraint into an equation by adding a **slack variable**: the unused part of the resource.

3x + 2y is at most 120 becomes 3x + 2y + s1 = 120, with s1 at least 0.

The objective Z = 4x + 3y is rewritten Z - 4x - 3y = 0. All variables, including slacks, are non-negative, and each right-hand side must be non-negative.

The starting plan is "do nothing": x = 0, y = 0, so each slack equals the whole resource (s1 = 120) and Z = 0. The first **tableau** is a table of these equations with a row for each constraint and a Z-row.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A slack of zero at the end means that resource has been completely used; a positive slack means some is left over.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a slack variable measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The amount of a resource left unused.

items.title: One simplex iteration, in five moves
items.core_explanation_md:
For a **maximisation**, repeat these moves until the Z-row has no negative numbers:

| Move | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Entering variable** | The column with the most negative Z-row entry (the best profit gain per unit) |
| 2. **Leaving variable** | For each row with a positive entry in that column, divide the solution value by that entry. The smallest ratio picks the row |
| 3. **Pivot entry** | Where the entering column meets the leaving row |
| 4. **New pivot row** | Divide the leaving row by the pivot entry |
| 5. **Other rows** (including Z) | Subtract (the row's entry in the entering column) times the new pivot row |

The smallest-ratio rule stops you from pushing a variable so far that some resource would go negative.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each iteration moves to a neighbouring corner of the feasible region with a profit at least as high. When no negative remains in the Z-row, no neighbouring corner is better.

self_check.prompt_text: Solution values 120 and 60, entering-column entries 3 and 1. Which row leaves?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ratios 40 and 60: the smaller is 40, so the first row leaves.

items.title: Reading the final tableau: scarce and abundant resources, shadow prices
items.core_explanation_md:
The last tableau tells you far more than the plan.

- **Basic variables** and the solution column give the optimal quantities and the maximum Z.
- A **slack variable that is basic with a positive value** marks an **abundant** resource: some is left over, so more of it would not help.
- A **slack equal to zero** marks a **scarce** resource: it is fully used and limits the profit.
- The Z-row entry under a slack variable is the **shadow price** of that resource: how much Z would rise for one more unit of it. Abundant resources have a shadow price of zero.

This is how a manager decides where extra capacity or funds would pay off.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Always read the slack from the tableau itself, not from memory of the problem: check the basic variables and their values. The courseware example illustrates why. Its final tableau has the slack of the third workshop equal to 6, but the accompanying text attributes the slack to the first workshop.

self_check.prompt_text: Optimum tableau: basic variables are x = 30, y = 15 and s3 = 25; the slack entries in the Z-row are 1.25, 0.25 and 0. Which resources are scarce, and what is each extra unit of the first worth?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The first two resources (their slacks are zero, non-basic) are scarce; the third (s3 = 25) is abundant. An extra unit of the first resource adds 1.25 to Z.

items.title: What simulation is, and when to use it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Simulation** means experimenting on a **model** of a system instead of on the system itself. You imitate how the system behaves, run it many times under assumed conditions, and watch what happens.

The model can be a set of equations, a physical model, a rehearsal, a computer graphic or a game. In banking and finance it is nearly always a computer model.

Why do it?

- The real experiment would be risky, costly, slow or disruptive.
- The problem is too large or too complex for a formula (queues at counters, inventory rules, forex and investment risk).
- You want to train people safely, as a driving simulator does.

The limit: a simulation is **only as good as its assumptions**. A neat result from a wrong model is still wrong.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Simulation is often used alongside statistics and management techniques, not instead of them. Statistics supplies the probability distributions that drive the model.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two reasons for simulating instead of experimenting on the real system, and one limit of simulation.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: the experiment would be risky, costly, disruptive or slow; or the problem is too complex for other methods. Limit: results are only as good as the model's assumptions.

items.title: Random-number intervals: turning probabilities into draws
items.core_explanation_md:
To make a computer or a table of random numbers behave like a real demand pattern, give each possible outcome a block of the numbers 00 to 99 **as large as its probability**.

| Demand | Probability | Cumulative | Random numbers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 35 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 00 to 09 (10 numbers) |
| 45 | 0.3 | 0.4 | 10 to 39 (30 numbers) |
| 55 | 0.2 | 0.6 | 40 to 59 (20 numbers) |
| 65 | 0.3 | 0.9 | 60 to 89 (30 numbers) |
| 75 | 0.1 | 1.0 | 90 to 99 (10 numbers) |

Each block starts where the previous one ends (cumulative probability times 100). A random number such as 52 lands in 40 to 59, so that day's demand is 55.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because every two-digit number is equally likely, an outcome with probability 0.3 is chosen 30 times in 100 over a long run. In a short run the proportions will not match exactly; that is natural sampling variation.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{interval for outcome } k:\ [\,100 F_{k-1},\ 100 F_k - 1\,],\quad F_k = \sum_{j \le k} p_j

variables.name: Cumulative probability up to outcome k
Block of two-digit random numbers assigned to outcome k

assumptions: Probabilities add to 1.
Random numbers are equally likely and independent.
common_errors: Making an interval too short or too long for its probability.
Overlapping intervals or leaving gaps.
Using three-digit numbers with two-digit intervals.

self_check.prompt_text: An outcome has probability 0.25 and the cumulative probability before it is 0.40. Which two-digit numbers are assigned to it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 40 to 64 (25 numbers, starting at 40).

items.title: Running a manual simulation, step by step
items.core_explanation_md:
Take a branch kiosk that buys a perishable item at a cost, sells it at a price and loses unsold stock each day. Each simulated day:

1. **Draw** a random number.
2. **Look up** its interval in the demand table and read off the demand.
3. **Sold quantity** = the smaller of demand and the quantity ordered.
4. **Profit** = sold x price - ordered x cost.

Repeat for many days, then average the daily profits. To compare two **ordering rules**, run both on the **same random numbers**, so that the difference comes from the rule and not from luck.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ordering more than demand wastes stock; ordering less loses sales. The simulation finds which rule balances the two over many days.

self_check.prompt_text: Why compare two ordering rules on the same set of random numbers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: So that both rules face the same demand sequence, and any difference in profit is due to the rules.

items.title: Simulation methodology: define, build, run, evaluate
items.core_explanation_md:
| Stage | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| **Define the problem** | State the objective; separate **controllable** variables (decision rule, order quantity) from **uncontrollable** ones (demand) |
| **Build the model** | Choose variables, parameters, decision rules, probability distributions and how **time** advances |
| **Run** | Set starting conditions and **run length**; run the model |
| **Evaluate** | Examine the results with statistical tests |
| **New experiment** | Change something and compare |

**Time**: with **fixed increments** the clock moves by a set step (hour, day, month); use when events occur regularly. With **variable increments** the clock jumps to the next event; use when events are infrequent (ordering only when stock falls to a level).

**Run length**: a fixed period; long enough to give large samples; or until equilibrium (simulated data match the historical frequencies).
items.expanded_explanation_md: A simulated clock is needed in either case. Models are custom-built for each problem, unlike linear programming, where the same structure is reused with new numbers.

self_check.prompt_text: Stock is reordered only when it falls to 100 units. Fixed or variable time increments?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Variable: events are infrequent and irregular, so the clock should jump to the next event.

items.title: When simulation helps and what it costs
items.core_explanation_md:
| Simulation is desirable when real experiments... | Simulation is preferable when a mathematical model... |
| --- | --- |
| would disrupt ongoing activities | is not available |
| would be too costly | is too complex or arduous to solve |
| need many observations over a long time | is beyond the available personnel |
| cannot replicate events exactly | is not robust enough to cover all factors of interest |
| do not allow control of key variables | |

**Drawbacks**: it takes time; it needs computer expertise; some problems are hard to quantify; and there are few firm rules about what to include in the model and how long to run it, so it is **more art than science**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the results come from random draws, they carry sampling variation. Longer runs reduce it but do not remove the need to check the assumptions.

self_check.prompt_text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of simulation.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Advantage: it lets you experiment without disrupting or risking the real system. Disadvantage: it is time consuming and needs expertise, with few rules for model design.

items.title: Why people are different from every other resource
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks buy the same software, rent similar premises and follow the same regulations. What they cannot copy from each other is their **people**. That is why human resources are the main differentiator of an organisation, and why organisations now care more about the **quality** of their people than the number.

What makes people management different from managing money or machines?

| Other resources | People |
| --- | --- |
| Passive: do not react to how they are treated | **React**: responses are neither standard nor uniform |
| Systems and infrastructure settle down | People management stays **dynamic** and never fully stabilises |
| Can be copied by competitors | Individual skills, knowledge and attitudes cannot be copied |

Even the best strategy fails if the people who must carry it out are not convinced. Changing habits and mindset is slow, which is why implementation is harder than design.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An organisation is first a **social system**: it combines people and technology. That is why human behaviour at work is a major subject of HR study.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two reasons people management is harder than managing physical resources.
self_check.expected_takeaway: People react to treatment and respond differently from one another, and people management never settles into a fixed system; physical resources are passive and can be standardised.

items.title: From administrative department to strategic partner
items.core_explanation_md:
HR has changed its place in the organisation.

| | Old perspective | Present perspective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standing | Necessary but unessential, even unproductive | Strategic partner and business catalyst |
| Work | Administration, welfare and record keeping | Talent, culture, capability and change |
| Source of wealth | Land and capital (earlier eras) | **Human capital** in the knowledge era |

What changed? Shifting workforce demographics, rapid technological change, a generation gap in work ethics and the globalisation of the economy altered how businesses operate, so people management had to change too.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Every era has a primary source of wealth: land in the agrarian era, and in the knowledge era the people who use technology: their skills, knowledge and attitudes make the difference.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the primary source of wealth creation in the knowledge era, according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Human capital.

items.title: What an organisation is, and the two streams of thought
items.core_explanation_md:
An **organisation** (in the courseware's quotation of Schein) is the rational coordination of the activities of many people to achieve a common, explicit purpose, through **division of labour and function** and a **hierarchy of authority and responsibility**.

- **Formal** organisation: goals, structure, roles and relationships are explicit and documented, to keep decisions consistent.
- **Informal** organisation: roles and relationships evolve from group processes.

Too much structure causes rigidity and slows decisions.

Two streams of thinking developed side by side:

1. how to **organise the activities** most systematically (the work);
2. how to understand the **individual's relation to work** (the person).

Early figures: **Robert Owen** (workers are "vital machines", so better conditions raise productivity) and **Charles Babbage** (division of labour, scientific principles of work).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The history of people management is the history of management thought: each theory of how to manage work carried an assumption about people.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two interdependent streams does the courseware identify?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How to organise activities systematically, and how to understand the individual's relation to work.

items.title: Scientific management and why it fell short
items.core_explanation_md:
**Frederick Taylor** (with Gantt and Gilbreth) built **scientific management** on division of labour and time-and-motion studies. Its three working assumptions:

1. Tasks can be broken into simple units that people can understand and perform.
2. People will do a given activity **in return for money**.
3. People must do what the organisation and its technology define.

**What it overlooked:** fatigue, boredom, the need to talk to colleagues, group dynamics and relationships. It treated people as replaceable, which helped fuel **labour unions** and unrest. It has little relevance today in a **VUCA** world (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The approach was productive for simple repetitive work, but it controlled only the activities strictly related to the work and let go of everything else people bring to it.

self_check.prompt_text: Which assumption of scientific management is most clearly contradicted by later motivation research?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That people work only for money; later researchers showed meaning, responsibility and achievement also motivate.

items.title: Hawthorne, human relations and the social man
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Hawthorne Studies** (Elton Mayo and colleagues, Western Electric, 1924-33) found that emotions, relationships and the meaning of work affect performance. The **human relations movement** that followed swapped the **rational-economic man** (works for pay, responds to logic of work design) for the **social man** (needs belonging, recognition and good relationships).

Later researchers (Argyris, Maslow, McGregor, Herzberg) pushed further: people are motivated by **more than money**. They want to find meaning in what they do, to carry responsibility and to feel a sense of achievement. If those are missing, performance suffers.

So people management had to provide those ingredients, and this started the **developmental approach**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This also explains why people management systems began to care for relationships with supervisors, colleagues and groups.

self_check.prompt_text: What replaced the "rational-economic man" in the human relations movement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The "social man", motivated by relationships and meaning as well as pay.

items.title: How people management became a function
items.core_explanation_md:
As organisations grew after the Industrial Revolution, specialised **departments** for finance, accounting and production appeared, and later one for **people**.

- Early forms: welfare or **social secretaries** to meet workers' needs and prevent unions; the **Time Office** in textile mills and factories; the **establishment section** in banks and commercial offices.
- The title **personnel officer** appeared in the 1960s (chemical and pharmaceutical industries).
- In India, Prof. A. K. Rice's 1952 group-behaviour experiment at Ahmedabad mills was a landmark.

**Core activities**: recruitment and selection; training and developing; performance appraisal; reward and compensation. **Added later**: manpower assessment, career management, succession planning, talent management.

Two traditions pulled in different directions, the **profit-minded** economics tradition and the **welfare** social-psychology tradition, until organisations accepted two goals: **productivity** and **maintenance** (employee satisfaction and wellness).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Policies that maximise one goal can damage the other, so organisations that ignore employee wellness harm their own sustainability.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four fundamental activities of people management and two of the later additions.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Recruitment and selection, training and developing, performance appraisal, reward and compensation; later manpower assessment, career management, succession planning, talent management (any two).

items.title: HRM, personnel management and HRD
items.core_explanation_md:
The function evolved by **adding** dimensions, never by throwing the old ones away. Its name changed from **Labour and Welfare** to **Personnel** to **HR**.

**HRM** is the **umbrella** for all people-related functions and a **line-and-staff** responsibility: every manager carries out part of it. In Sheth's words, as the courseware quotes him, it treats people as stakeholders whose development and growth are critical, seeks to harmonise their interests with the organisation's, and rests on human sensitivity, trust and participative management.

**How the functions are classified:**

| Classification | Groups |
| --- | --- |
| De'Cenzo | Acquisition, Development, Motivation, Maintenance |
| Pareek and Rao | Planning and Administration, HRD, Job and Salary, Workers Affairs |
| Mankidy | Administrative, Developmental, Preventive |

**Administration and maintenance**: acquisition, promotion, administration, salary and long-term benefits, grievance and discipline. **HRD**: induction, development and growth, appraisal and counselling, career planning.

**HRM and HRD**: no conflict in structure or functions; the difference is **approach and emphasis**. HRM covers routine people functions; HRD emphasises organisation-wide interventions (climate, employee and organisational development tied to goals, change management) and building human capital. HRD is sometimes treated as the most significant subsystem of HRM.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Exam answers often hinge on this point: HRM and HRD are related, HRD sits within the HRM umbrella, and their difference lies in emphasis, not in separate departments.

self_check.prompt_text: Is succession planning an administrative or a developmental function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Developmental (HRD): it identifies and prepares people to replace key functionaries.

items.title: The role of HR professionals: five roles and the line manager
items.core_explanation_md:
As the function matured from personnel to HRM and HRD, its professionals moved from policing attendance and discipline to developing people and systems.

**Pareek and Rao's five roles** (as the courseware reports them):

| Role | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| **Supportive** | Strengthen operating and executive levels |
| **Systems development and research** | Systems that deal with people, their problems and organisational dynamics |
| **Managerial** | Plan manpower, recruit, place, retain, motivate, appraise, plan growth |
| **Developing competence** | Technical, managerial and processing competence; coping competence |
| **Process** | Culture and values, diagnosing organisation-level problems, corrective steps |

**Line managers** are the **delivery points** for people management, including development, so HR cannot be delinked from them. Whether HR heads must be trained specialists or can be line managers with the right outlook is an open debate; what decides success is the HR philosophy (values), which is not the property of any one profession.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Statutory obligations and strong unions made HR a specialist function in banks during the 1960s to 1980s: industrial relations and disciplinary enquiries needed legal knowledge.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the five roles concerns culture, values and corrective steps at organisation level?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The process role.

items.title: What makes an effective HR professional: attributes and competency models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Attributes** (Pareek and Rao): technical (appraisal systems, tests, behavioural sciences, career planning, counselling, behavioural research); managerial (organising ability, systems development skills); and **personality** (initiative, faith in human beings, positive attitude, concern for excellence and for people, teamwork, interest in learning). The personality group matters most: without initiative, faith in people, concern for employees' development and teamwork, the technical knowledge achieves little.

**Competency models:**

| Model | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **CII HR Competency Model** | **19** competencies for HR heads: **9 behavioural** (communication, initiative, drive, creativity, self-confidence, teamwork, influence, problem solving, inter-personal skills) and **10 functional** (business knowledge, change management, diversity management, service orientation, execution excellence, financial perspective, building expertise, personal credibility, relationship management, strategic thinking and alignment) |
| **SHRM Competency Model** | **9**: Leadership and Navigation, Ethical Practice, Business Acumen, Relationship Management, Consultation, Critical Evaluation, Global and Cultural Effectiveness, Communication, HR expertise |

In banks, HR is generally a generalist cadre posting rather than a professional specialisation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A successful HR professional is expected to be free from bias (honest, fearless, with a sense of justice), skilled in human relations and counselling, and willing to pass on credit and own up to failures.

self_check.prompt_text: How many competencies are in the CII HR Competency Model, and how do they divide?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 19: nine behavioural and ten functional.

items.title: Strategic HRM: linking people to business strategy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Strategic HRM** is the process of using employees' knowledge, skills and abilities in **formulating and carrying out** the business strategy. More broadly it links HRM with the organisation's strategic objectives to improve business performance, build culture and foster innovation and flexibility. It is **proactive**, and employees who help form strategy are more committed to it.

**Three HR roles** (courseware chart):

| Role | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Core people** | Selection, orientation, career development, motivation, compensation, welfare, retention and termination |
| **Organisational value-add** | HR technology services, a learning work environment, organisational development and consulting |
| **Business transformation** | A flexible work culture, aligning HR with business strategy, implementing change, measuring return on investment in human capital |

**Ulrich's four mandates:** partner with senior and line managers in strategy execution; expert in how work is organised (administrative efficiency); champion for employees; agent of continuous transformation.

A **competency gap** is the difference between what the present systems can do and what operations require; strategic HR identifies it and closes it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Compare with the old picture of HR as "policy police" and regulatory watchdog handling paperwork on hiring and firing.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two of Ulrich's four mandates.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: partner in strategy execution; expert in organising work efficiently; champion for employees; agent of continuous transformation.

items.title: New roles for HR professionals in banks
items.core_explanation_md:
Under strategic HRM, a bank's HR professionals move from being the bank's **conscience** (reactive, and proactive when needed) to **strategic business partners and enablers**.

- **Delegate day-to-day employee issues to line managers**, who act as local HR administrators.
- HR professionals become a **centre of excellence**, concentrating on **core policies** of general application.
- HR should be the **last, not the first**, point of contact on an employee-specific issue.
- They need **business knowledge**, understanding of **business process re-engineering** and **return on investment in human capital**, and **information technology** skills.
- Education: relevant professional programmes (such as a Master of Human Resource Management) and continuous learning through seminars and training.
- Focus on **internal customers** (employees) and on delivering value to the **external customer** too.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The old model, where only HR handled employee issues and line managers just extracted work, is described as out-lived.

self_check.prompt_text: In the new model, who is the first point of contact for an employee-specific issue?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The line manager; HR is the last, not the first, point of contact.

items.title: Development of HR functions in India
items.core_explanation_md:
India followed a path similar to the West, shaped by British rule and the world wars.

| Stage | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Independence era | **Labour welfare officers** under the **Factories Act**: recruiting, muster rolls and leave records, canteens, discipline |
| From the 1950s | **Industrial Disputes Act 1947** added legalistic duties: charge sheets, domestic enquiries, conciliation proceedings |
| 1960s | Demand for personnel specialists; professional bodies **IIPM** (1947) and **NILM**, merged in **1982** as **NIPM**; no academic requirement |
| Early exemplars | J. N. Tata and TISCO: proactive human-factor practices |
| Government legislation | Article 16(1) equal opportunity; Employment Exchanges Act 1959; Apprentices Act 1961; Bonded Labour System Act 1976; Child Labour Act 1986; Interstate Migrant Workmen Act 1979 |
| 1980s | **HRD** approach, pioneered by **Udai Pareek and T V Rao**; banks that began HRD processes include SBI, State Bank of Patiala, Bank of Baroda and Canara Bank; National HRD Network (1985); ISTD (1970) |
| Recent | Diversity, gender parity, mentoring, safety, AI in recruitment, HR analytics, employer branding |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites these facts as reported; some of the Acts have since been replaced or amended, so treat them as a historical account.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two institutes merged in 1982 to form NIPM?
self_check.expected_takeaway: IIPM and NILM.

items.title: Why development matters: people, jobs and the cost of skills
items.core_explanation_md:
Industrial work once treated people as substitutes for machines. Later thinking restored the human side: make work interesting and meaningful, recognise feelings and needs, and shape the job so that it satisfies people as well as output goals.

What do people value in a job? **Variety, challenge, good pay, security, autonomy and pleasant co-workers**, together with a sense that they are treated justly. Workers who are happy at work tend to be creative and committed.

Two hard business facts follow:

- Organisational goals are reached only if people at every level have the right **knowledge, skills, temperament and attitude**. As jobs grow complex, "anyone can do any job" no longer holds.
- When the skills are missing there are two routes: **upgrade the skills of existing staff**, or **hire new people** with the skills. The courseware notes that acquiring new people **always costs more** than upgrading existing workers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the economic case for HRD: investing in the people already in the bank is usually cheaper than replacing them.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two ways to close a skills gap, and say which is usually cheaper.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Upgrade the skills of existing employees, or recruit people with the skills; upgrading is usually cheaper.

items.title: The banking context that shaped HRD
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes how bank HR had to change over decades:

| Period | Pressure | Effect on HR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1970s to 1980s | Growth in the HRD idea | HRD moved beyond mere training |
| 1990s | Computerisation, cost reduction, outsourcing | Training for computer skills; fear among seniors who lacked them |
| 2000s to 2020 | Liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation; competition from foreign and new private banks | Customer service skills; analytics; restructuring |

**Bank responses:** core banking operations, business process re-engineering, voluntary retirement schemes, training and retraining, lateral recruitment of specialists, customer relationship management, new delivery channels, back offices and data centres, outsourcing.

**Consolidation:** the Narasimham Committee mooted mergers; five SBI associate banks merged with SBI; Vijaya and Dena Banks merged with Bank of Baroda; in 2019 the merger of ten public sector banks into four was announced. Merger benefits can be counted in profit figures, but the **human impact** cannot be measured in financial numbers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These changes needed carefully thought-out HR policies to help existing staff adapt and learn new skills.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the human impact of a bank merger not be captured in financial figures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It concerns people: roles, relationships, fears and the need to learn new skills, which are not measured by profitability.

items.title: Job analysis: what it is and what it feeds
items.core_explanation_md:
**Job analysis** is a technique for listing what a task or job requires. Work is the pivot of development, so a good HR manager knows each job well: the activities in it and the kind of person who suits it.

Traditionally it had **three parts**: job description, job specification and job evaluation. Because jobs became complex and are tied to the wage structure, **job evaluation is now treated as a separate exercise**, and job analysis concentrates on the first two:

- **Job description**: the activities involved.
- **Job specification**: what the person needs (qualification and attributes).

The three primary types of data are **work activities, worker attributes and work context**.

**What job analysis feeds:** manpower planning, recruitment and selection, learning and development, performance management, reward and compensation, talent management and succession planning, career planning. It is the basic framework for most HR systems.
items.expanded_explanation_md: **Job evaluation** compares jobs by their activities and responsibilities, their importance relative to other jobs, the qualifications required and the working conditions, so it underlies wage settlements.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two parts does job analysis now mainly consist of, and where has job evaluation gone?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Job description and job specification; job evaluation is treated as an independent exercise.

items.title: Task, job, position and role
items.core_explanation_md:
Everyday speech mixes these words. The courseware, following Pareek and Rao, separates them.

| Term | Meaning | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Task** | A basic element needing one person to achieve a specific product | Isolates the person |
| **Job** | A complex system of tasks that achieves an overall product | Still treats relationships as irrelevant |
| **Position** | A place in a hierarchy; those below report to those above | Can make one person powerful over others and dehumanise |
| **Role** | The pattern of **mutual expectations** between job holder, self and others; socio-psychological | The concept HRD relies on |

Task, job and position treat people as isolated or as machines. **Role** puts the individual into a complex relationship with the job, with self and with others.

The **Role Analysis Technique (RAT)** clarifies role expectations and obligations of team members to improve team effectiveness. When a role is analysed, the **Key Performance Areas (KPA)** and the critical attributes needed to perform effectively are identified.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a bank, a branch manager's role includes expectations from customers, staff, controllers and the regional head, not just a list of tasks.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of task, job, position and role is the most relevant for HRD, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Role, because it takes the individual into a complex set of mutual expectations rather than treating the person as an isolated performer or a means to a product.

items.title: Collecting job data and writing the description and specification
items.core_explanation_md:
**Sources:** the **job holder** (first-hand, but limited view; validate), the **supervisor** (broader view; validates and may redesign), **customers' feedback** (valuable where customer satisfaction decides success) and **experts or job analysts**.

**Methods:**

| Method | Strength | Caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Interview** | The most popular; gives a list of technical and behavioural skills | Build trust, assure that it will not harm the career, collect facts rather than opinions |
| **Questionnaire** | Economical and faster for many job holders | Make it simple, in a language people are comfortable with |
| **Observation** (with work sampling) | Detailed, accurate data on activities and methods | More time consuming; the person knows they are watched |

**Job description:** identification, summary, **duties performed** (the heart: what, how and why), supervision given and received, relations to other jobs, machines tools and materials, working conditions.

**Job specification:** educational qualification, professional qualification, experience, knowledge and skills, personality characteristics, physical make-up, interests, other requirements.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the job holder knows the job best but has a limited view, the information is validated through the supervisor and, where relevant, customers and experts.

self_check.prompt_text: Which job-data method is most economical when many job holders perform similar jobs?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The questionnaire.

items.title: Learning, training, education and development
items.core_explanation_md:
**Learning** is the acquisition of knowledge, skills or attitudes through experience, study or teaching. **Development** broadens and deepens knowledge in line with one's development goals.

Nadler's three-way label for organisational activities:

| Activity | Aim | Who is mainly responsible |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Training** | Learning for the **present job** | The immediate superior |
| **Education** | Learning to prepare for a **different but identified job** | The central department or HR functionary |
| **Development** | Growth of the individual, **not tied to a specific present or future job** | The central department or HR functionary |

Why separate them? The **objectives** differ (training should show up in performance; development has no direct performance impact), the **expectations** of the individual and the superior become clear, and **responsibility** is assigned. The labels matter less than using them **uniformly** in the organisation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Other writers use the words differently, calling future-oriented learning development and non-job-specific learning education. Check which usage a question follows.

self_check.prompt_text: A clerk is sent on a course for a post of assistant manager, an identified different job. Training, education or development?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Education (learning to prepare for a different but identified job).

items.title: How adults learn
items.core_explanation_md:
Adults are not big children. **Andragogy** (adult learning) is more **learner-centred**; **pedagogy** (child learning) is teacher-centred. Treating adult learners like children by the pedagogical model does not give the desired results.

**Seven principles of adult learning:** self-directed; transformational; experiential; mentorship; orientation (reframing emotions and assumptions about experience); motivation (mostly internal); readiness (shaped by life experience and change).

**Three families of learning theory** (Knowles):

| Theory | View of the learner | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mechanistic (behaviourist)** | Passive; conditioned to respond to stimuli | Produce the right response |
| **Cognitive** | A brain that can think critically and solve problems | Teach the brain to engage in such thinking |
| **Organismic (humanistic)** | Has the freedom to learn | Develop each person's full potential |

**Common assumptions** (Decenzo and Robbins): learning improves when the learner is **motivated**, needs **feedback**, is helped by **reinforcement**, improves with **practice**, and must be **transferable to the job**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: All three theory families are relevant in an organisation because all three kinds of learning situation occur there. Training for senior executives, for example, may focus on vision and strategy rather than skills.

self_check.prompt_text: Which learning theory family treats the learner as passive and conditioned to respond to stimuli?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Mechanistic (behaviourist) theories.

items.title: Systematic approach to training: needs and plan
items.core_explanation_md:
A planned training system follows five steps:

1. **Training needs analysis (TNA)**
2. **Training plan**
3. **Conduct** of the training
4. **Evaluation** of the programmes and the plan
5. **Selection and development of trainers**

**TNA** looks at present and future needs. **Present** gaps show in appraisals, productivity norms, rejects, accidents and mistakes, inspection reports. **Future** needs come from the bank's business plan (new products, technology, expansion). Training cannot cure every problem: poor technology, outdated processes and poor working conditions are not training problems. TNA data should define the need, identify the solution, specify who needs training and give planning details.

The **annual training plan** fixes: how many programmes (internal and external), which levels of staff, which subjects (and which are left for later), the resources, and arrangements for contingencies. **On-the-job** methods: apprenticeship, job instruction training, understudy assignment, programmed instruments, job rotation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Whether training is delivered in-house or at external institutions, the same five steps are needed. Most banks run in-house training for bank-specific skills and send people outside for specialised training.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is NOT solved by training: low skill, or an outdated process?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An outdated process: training cannot fix problems caused by poor technology, outdated processes or poor working conditions.

items.title: Conducting and evaluating training, and the trainers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Conducting** a programme starts with **objectives**: they decide the content, the time (a skill needs practice time) and the **method**. The profile of the group matters: people with no work experience cannot discuss work cases. Methods range from readings and lecturettes through group discussion, case studies and role plays to simulation games, assessment centres and small-group work. The more **interactive** the method, the more the trainer needs the ability to handle the data the group generates.

**Evaluating** training works at four levels (similar to Kirkpatrick):

| Level | Question |
| --- | --- |
| **Reaction** | Did participants find it favourable, engaging and relevant? |
| **Learning** | Did they acquire the intended knowledge, skills and attitudes (tested before and after)? |
| **Behaviour** | Did they apply it back on the job? |
| **Functioning (results)** | Did the organisation benefit, for example return on training investment? |

The fourth level is the hardest to measure, because benefits are hard to separate from other causes.

**Trainers:** operational managers know the work but may take a narrow, in-bred view; professional trainers bring a fresh view but may lack industry knowledge. A combination often works, and either type needs skill development.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each higher level is harder to measure but more valuable: a well-liked course (reaction) may still not change behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: List the four levels of training evaluation in order.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Reaction, learning, behaviour, functioning (results).

items.title: Support systems that make learning and development work
items.core_explanation_md:
Training alone does not develop people. Three supports decide whether it does:

| Support | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Performance appraisal link** | Information from appraisals feeds learning needs; without the flow, training becomes a **mechanical** exercise |
| **HR information system (HRIS)** | Holds on-the-job experience, placements, skills and training attended: a **database for training** |
| **Organisational culture** | The most critical: superiors, HR and top management must **act** as if training matters |

A superior who hesitates to relieve a subordinate for training, or a top team that refuses budget and flexibility, wipes out the purpose of training. One company made the appraiser act as mentor and take on the appraisee's training in agreed areas, written into the appraiser's **key result area**.

**Beliefs top management should repeat** (Rao, as reported): people are the most important asset and can be developed without limit; a healthy climate (openness, enthusiasm, trust, mutuality, collaboration) is essential; commitment grows from belonging; every manager is responsible for developing subordinates; senior managers should give HRD more attention.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Contradictory signals are the usual failure: a policy that praises training while managers refuse to release staff.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the three support systems does the courseware call the most critical?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The organisational culture, in which superiors, HR and top management show that training matters.

items.title: What an attitude is, and its three components
items.core_explanation_md:
An **attitude** is a **persistent tendency to feel and behave in a particular way** towards some object: a person, a bank, a product, a practice, an idea.

Three features: it **persists** unless something changes it; it lies on a **continuum** from very favourable to very unfavourable; and it is **directed at an object** about which the person has perceptions, feelings and beliefs, which can make opinions emotionally charged.

Attitudes are **not** built on complete, objective information, which is why two people can hold different attitudes to the same thing.

| Component | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emotional** | Feelings: positive, neutral or negative | "I dislike touring" |
| **Informational** | Beliefs and information, perhaps inaccurate | A manager believes two weeks of training is enough when four are needed |
| **Behavioural** | The tendency to act | The manager allows only two weeks |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The informational component may rest on insufficient observation or opinion, which is why attitudes can be wrong yet still shape behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager believes a trainee needs only two weeks; four are really needed. Which component of the attitude is this?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The informational component (a belief that may not be correct).

items.title: Why attitudes matter at work: four functions
items.core_explanation_md:
Why study attitudes? They **predict behaviour** (a negative reaction to a new work rule may show up as absenteeism), help people **adapt** to the work environment, and are weighed when people are **selected and posted**. It is easier to impart skills than to change an attitude, and a negatively oriented employee tends to find fault in every solution.

Attitudes serve four functions:

| Function | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Adjustment** | Helps people adjust to the work environment | Fair treatment by the boss produces a positive attitude to supervision |
| **Ego-defensive** | Protects self-image | An older manager whose decisions are challenged turns negative towards younger officers |
| **Value-expression** | Expresses one's values | A believer in the work ethic voices it to subordinates |
| **Knowledge** | Gives standards and frames of reference to make sense of events | A union officer's distrust makes everything management says "a pack of lies" |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The knowledge function shows that attitudes act as filters: they help us make sense of events even when the picture they give is inaccurate.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager who dislikes criticism from a younger subordinate develops a negative view of all younger officers. Which function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ego-defensive.

items.title: Changing attitudes: barriers and methods
items.core_explanation_md:
Attitudes can be changed, though with difficulty that depends on how deep-rooted and emotionally charged they are.

**Two main barriers:** **prior commitment** (the person is committed to a course of action) and **lack or distortion of information**.

**Ways to change:**

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **New information** | May change beliefs and so the attitude |
| **Fear** | Moderate fear tends to work; **low** fear is ignored; **high** fear is rejected as too threatening |
| **Resolving attitude-behaviour discrepancy** | After choosing one of two jobs, people come to value the chosen one and devalue the other |
| **Friends, peers, opinion leaders** | Leaders who build trust and appear rational and caring shape followers |
| **A friendly, interested manager** | Learns the employee's motives and learning needs |
| **Co-opting** | Involve a dissatisfied person in improving things (for example the welfare committee) |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Co-opting works because, once people see how hard the problem is and how decisions are made, they are likely to change their view.

self_check.prompt_text: Which level of fear is most likely to change an attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Moderate fear: low fear is ignored and high fear is rejected as too threatening.

items.title: Careers: life stages, career roles and patterns
items.core_explanation_md:
A **career** is the sequence and variety of work roles a person undertakes over life; **career development** is the lifelong process of managing learning, work and transitions; a **career path** is a sequence of jobs leading to short- and long-term goals. People who find that expected advancement is not coming on time become **disillusioned**, **frustrated** or **alienated**.

**Life stages:** Erikson (adult stages): adolescence (ego identity), young adulthood (relationships), adulthood (guiding the next generation), maturity (ego integrity). Levinson: a career or personal transition every five to seven years.

**Career roles** (Dalton, Thompson and Price):

| Role | Position |
| --- | --- |
| **Apprentice** | Routine work under a mentor; some dependency |
| **Colleague** | Independent contribution, still subordinate |
| **Mentor** | Complex functions; develops ideas, manages others, answerable for subordinates' work |
| **Sponsor** | Top management; long-term direction; chooses people to support |

**Career concepts** (Driver): **linear** (up the hierarchy), **steady state** (skills up, not rank), **transitory** (job to job), **spiral** (new type of work after moving up). A **plateau** means staying at a level.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Schein's three directions of movement: **vertical** (up), **circumferential** (across functions), **radial** (towards the centre).

self_check.prompt_text: Which career role is part of top management and chooses people to support its influence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sponsor.

items.title: Career paths in an organisation, and career anchors
items.core_explanation_md:
When movements across **branches and functions** and up through **levels** are laid down in a logical sequence, the organisation has a **career path**: a destination, the distance, the crossroads and the **signboards** (criteria for eligibility to move). In a bank: apprentice assignments in different branches, then a colleague role, a spell at controlling offices, larger branches, and as regional manager a mentor role.

**A caution:** the structure is a pyramid. Fewer posts exist at higher levels, so a path does not guarantee smooth movement. Competition, supersession and bottlenecks cause frustration; people must be helped to accept that not everyone reaches the top.

**Career anchors** (Schein) are a person's self-concept about the **work they want**, formed over time from self-perceived **talents and abilities**, **motives and needs**, and **attitudes and values**. Five anchors:

1. Technical/functional competence
2. Managerial competence
3. Security
4. Creativity
5. Autonomy
items.expanded_explanation_md: The **internal career** is the individual's own self-concept of what he or she is good at (career anchors); the **external career** is the set of opportunities offered by education, society and organisations.

self_check.prompt_text: Name Schein's five career anchors.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Technical/functional competence, managerial competence, security, creativity, autonomy.

items.title: Career path planning as an HR system
items.core_explanation_md:
**Career planning** is systematically matching career goals and individual capabilities with opportunities. In a bank it is an HRD subsystem linking manpower planning, job rotation, transfer, placement, training and appraisal. It structures employees' **aspirations** for upward movement and **moderates unrealistic ones**. It does **not** commit management to promote anyone: the path is a **facility for growth, not a right**.

**What the organisation should do:** state the policy and benchmarks; encourage growth and discourage superiors who suppress it; make the path **known from entry**, with performance feedback; apply it **without bias**; keep it **flexible**.

**Four steps to chalk out the path:**

1. **Define the career stages** (apprentice, colleague, mentor, sponsor) against organisational levels.
2. **Identify core jobs at each level**: comparable jobs form **job families**, and each person should hold at least one job from the family.
3. **Define transparent criteria** (weightages and measurement) for each next level.
4. **Place the person in the next role**, with training and counselling. Colleague-to-mentor needs a **developmental** outlook; mentor-to-sponsor needs **conceptual skills** (visioning, planning, creative problem solving).

**Multiple careers:** specialist functions (finance, HR, marketing, planning, quality, IT) offer expert careers; in **flatter organisations** the spiral concept becomes the ideal, and Schein recommends **career counselling workshops** to help people see their anchors.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because top positions are few, a sensible career plan also moderates expectations and develops expertise across several areas.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two things should a transparent career criterion for the next level include?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The criteria (what is expected) and their weightages and measurement (how it is assessed).

items.title: Self-development and personal efficacy
items.core_explanation_md:
Everyone has a **patent self** (the external identity: appearance, role) and an **inner self** (values, strengths, weaknesses). First impressions are of the patent self; closeness reveals the inner one.

**Self-development** is the continuing effort to become a mature personality who can handle varied tasks with relative ease, by discovering and using one's potential.

Why it is the organisation's business: structures and reporting lines can be changed on paper, but unless people's **mindsets** change the change is only cosmetic (Pareek). Organisations that want to become learning organisations must make the individual the focal point of self-renewal.

**Personal efficacy** depends on four factors: **motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation**.

The courseware covers self-development at three levels: **individual** (motivational pattern, locus of control, power bases), **interpersonal** (interpersonal needs, transactional analysis) and **group** (effective membership of a work group), plus **emotional intelligence** and **morale**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Individuals need to see that unless they change and develop, they will become a misfit as the environment changes.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four factors that contribute to personal efficacy.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation.

items.title: Motivational pattern, locus of control and power bases
items.core_explanation_md:
**Motivational pattern.** People work for money, status, appreciation, satisfaction and self-growth; the mix keeps changing. Awareness of one's own goals and need bases helps people pick suitable development. HR policy must stay sensitive to changing needs.

**Locus of control** (Leftcourt; Levenson):

| Internal | External |
| --- | --- |
| "I can determine events" | "Luck, destiny, other people decide" |
| Takes initiative, looks for resources, anticipates | Waits for outside forces |

Someone with an external locus can be re-oriented through feedback that credits success to **their own** efforts and ideas, not luck or an easy task.

**Power** (Kotter: potential to get others to do what you want). French and Raven: coercive, legitimate, referent, expert (and reward). The courseware also describes:

| Power | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Coercive | Threat or punishment |
| Legitimate (position) | The position and delegation, not the person |
| Reward | Ability to reward, including praise |
| Referent | Respect; followers model the manager |
| Expert | Knowledge, skills, experience, credibility |
| Knowledge | Knowing the job, people and organisation |
| Reflected | Closeness to a power source |
| Charismatic | Emotional attraction of extraordinary characteristics |
| Emotional | Personal relationships and emotional bonds |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Awareness of the power one has, and how much more is needed, is part of being an effective leader. Power is also used in deciding who is rewarded and how.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager's power comes from her post in the organisation and would pass to anyone appointed to it. Which base?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Legitimate (position) power.

items.title: Interpersonal needs and transactional analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interpersonal needs** (Schutz): **inclusion** (to be part of), **control** (to influence or be influenced) and **affection** (to be liked). Knowing your own pattern helps you see how you interact with colleagues, subordinates and superiors.

**Transactional analysis** (Eric Berne) studies a **transaction**: a stimulus and its response. A personality blends three **ego states**:

| Ego state | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Parent** | Regulates and nurtures; *nurturing* (caring) or *critical* (judgemental); right and wrong messages from elders |
| **Adult** | Logical, rational, unemotional; collects information; solves problems |
| **Child** | Natural impulses; creativity, curiosity, enjoyment (adapted child, natural child, little professor) |

**Complementary** transactions (Parent to Child and Child back to Parent; Adult to Adult) keep communication flowing. **Crossed** transactions (for example Parent to Child answered by Parent to Child) **block** it and should be avoided.

**Life positions** (Harris): I am OK, you are OK; I am OK, you are not OK; I am not OK, you are OK; I am not OK, you are not OK. Pareek developed twelve influencing styles, six in the OK states and six in the not OK states.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The aim is not to eliminate the Child (it carries creativity) but to be aware of which ego state is active and to choose behaviour that fits the situation.

self_check.prompt_text: A supervisor says "You people are always late" (Parent to Child) and the officer replies "And you never listen" (Parent to Child). What kind of transaction is it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A crossed transaction: both speak from Parent to Child, so communication is blocked.

items.title: Working in teams, group stages and the Johari Window
items.core_explanation_md:
A **team** is a group whose members are highly interdependent and aim at a goal. **Group dynamics** (Kurt Lewin, 1930s) studies how groups form, their structure and processes, and how they affect individuals and the organisation.

Members play two sets of roles: **task roles** (getting the job done) and **maintenance roles** (keeping the group cohesive: listening, respecting views). **Consensus** is not compromise or majority rule; it means debating the pros and cons with respect for each member.

**Stages** (as the courseware lists them): **forming** (awareness), **storming** (conflict), **norming** (cooperation), **conforming** (adjustment), **performing** (productivity).

**Self-awareness** can be helped by a **SWOT of oneself** and the **Johari Window** (Luft and Ingham):

| | Known to self | Not known to self |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Known to others** | **Arena** (open) | **Blind** |
| **Not known to others** | **Closed** (hidden) | **Dark** (unknown) |

To **enlarge the Arena**, seek feedback (reduces the Blind area) and disclose yourself (reduces the Closed area). A bigger Arena builds trust and effectiveness.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The usual textbook model of group stages is forming, storming, norming and performing; the courseware adds "conforming" between norming and performing.

self_check.prompt_text: A colleague tells you that you interrupt people, which you did not know. Which Johari window did this move into the Arena?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Blind window (known to others but not to self).

items.title: Emotional intelligence and morale
items.core_explanation_md:
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capability to manage your own emotions and influence those of others. Goleman argues that IQ alone does not predict success; EI, unlike IQ, grows through adulthood and can be learned. Five components:

| Component | Meaning | Elements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Self-awareness** | Recognising your moods, emotions, drives | Emotional awareness, self-assessment, self-confidence |
| **Self-regulation** | Controlling disruptive impulses; thinking before acting | Self-control, trustworthiness, conscientiousness, adaptability, innovation |
| **Self-motivation** | Passion beyond money or status | Achievement drive, commitment, initiative, optimism |
| **Empathy** | Understanding others' emotions | Understanding and developing others, service orientation, leveraging diversity, political awareness |
| **Social skills** | Managing relationships | Influence, communication, conflict management, leadership, change catalyst, building bonds, collaboration, team capabilities |

**Morale** is the general mood of a person or group: confident, motivated, willing. High morale shows as confidence, cheerfulness, discipline and willingness; it depends on motivation, rewards and recognition. **Poor morale** lowers productivity and revenue and raises turnover.

**Boosters** include communicating often, welcoming ideas, recognising and sharing success, surveys and open-door access, an open forum, thank-you notes, a daily huddle, and measuring morale regularly. For negativity from faulty information, solve the problem systematically with the people affected.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites a Sirota Consulting finding (low-morale companies' share prices rose 3 per cent against an industry average of 16 per cent) without further detail; treat it as illustrative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five components of emotional intelligence.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Self-awareness, self-regulation, self-motivation, empathy and social skills.

items.title: Talent management: attract, develop, retain
items.core_explanation_md:
**Talent** has three Cs: **competence** (the head: being able to do), **commitment** (hands and feet: action) and **contribution** (the heart: doing it).

**Talent management** is anticipating the human capital an organisation will need and planning to meet it. The term was coined by McKinsey and Company after a 1997 study. It covers **acquiring, developing and retaining** talent. The courseware lists five interdependent elements:

1. Attracting the right talent
2. Onboarding
3. Creating a talent pool
4. Designing the talent career path
5. Retaining talent

Why it matters in banks: demand for skilled people exceeds supply. The courseware argues that new-generation employees are more loyal to their **careers than to their employer**, that turnover among highly talented staff will rise, and that they seek leisure, freedom at work, flexi-time and work-life balance.

Surveys of corporate talent management departments found its work included **succession planning, assessment, development and high-potential management**; compensation was not part of it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If one element is out of step (for example attracting people without a career path for them), the whole structure weakens.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three Cs of talent in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competence, commitment and contribution.

items.title: Succession planning and replacement planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Succession planning** identifies and develops people who can take over from leaders who leave, retire or die. It is a business strategy for passing leadership roles on, by developing internal people with the potential to fill key positions.

| | Replacement planning | Succession (talent-pool) planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Specific **back-up candidates** for given senior positions (the "truck scenario") | A **pipeline** of feeder groups through the leadership levels |
| Courseware view | Research suggests little effect on outcomes | The heart of effective succession planning |

**Objectives:** identify people with potential; give critical development experiences; engage leaders in developing high-potential staff; build a database for staffing key jobs.

**Benefits:** better commitment and retention; meets career development expectations; counters the rising cost and difficulty of external recruitment.

It is an integral part of **career planning** and touches recruitment, training and performance management.

**Banks:** the courseware finds Indian banks' approach (sporadic exposures, quick promotion to fill gaps) **inadequate**, and calls for a comprehensive strategy with **assessment centres and 360-degree feedback**, and management development programmes for senior executives focused on high-end **soft skills**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware quotes survey figures on small firms' lack of written succession plans and on how often firms pick the wrong people for manager roles; they illustrate the problem but were not independently checked.

self_check.prompt_text: How does replacement planning differ from succession planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Replacement planning names specific back-up candidates for specific positions; succession planning builds feeder groups across the whole leadership pipeline.
